interest: Shows 1941 ONI surveillance of Japanese-American mutual-aid societies, and a 1940 account of Grew sparring with Matsuoka at a luncheon.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.43, covering September 1940 to February 1942) documents Japanese societies and bilateral cultural and political organizations operating in Japan and the United States on the eve of and during the opening months of World War II. The centerpiece of the file is an extensive February 1942 Counter-Intelligence Section report from the Office of Naval Intelligence evaluating Japanese prefectural, regional, and overseas societies (such as Kenjin Kai and Kaigai Kyokai) in the United States, investigating their historical ties to Japanese emigration, suspected links to Tokyo's wartime propaganda and financial appeals, and providing an extensive geographical directory of West Coast branches. The file also contains diplomatic correspondence and cross-reference records regarding the America-Japan Society in Tokyo, including Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's reports on leadership elections and high-profile diplomatic luncheons featuring Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, as well as an eyewitness letter by American legal scholar Thomas L. Blakemore describing the interplay between Matsuoka and Grew as the bilateral relationship deteriorated.

subfiles.about: Intelligence report examining the history, organization, activities, propaganda ties, and local branch directory of Japanese prefectural, regional, and overseas societies in the United States.
subfiles.from: Counter-Intelligence Section, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: This comprehensive intelligence study by the Counter-Intelligence Section of the Office of Naval Intelligence investigates the background and functions of Japanese prefectural, regional, and overseas organizations (Kenjin Kai, Kaigai Kyokai, etc.) in the United States and its territories. Drawing from the 'History of Japanese Residents in America' published by the Japanese Association of America, the study traces how these bodies originated around 1900 as mutual-aid societies before developing close ties with Japanese colonization bodies and government propaganda programs, including donations to Tokyo's war chest and participation in the 1940 2600th Anniversary Celebration. While observing pre-war moves by some branches to demonstrate American loyalty and post-Pearl Harbor voluntary disbandments, the report concludes that their members warrant suspicion due to high proportions of aliens, exposure to Tokyo propaganda, and leadership ties to detained individuals. The report concludes with an extensive geographic roster detailing dozens of prefectural and regional associations with their street addresses in California, Oregon, Washington, Utah, and Hawaii.
subfiles.title: Study of Japanese Prefectural, Regional and Overseas Societies
